title: Count Pairs With XOR in a Range
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair directly versus a bitwise binary trie with an at-most-threshold subtraction.

content.title: Count Pairs With XOR in a Range

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and two integers low and high, return the number of index pairs (i, j) with i less than j such that low is less than or equal to (nums[i] XOR nums[j]), which is less than or equal to high.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","nums array, low, high"],["Output","Count of pairs whose XOR falls within [low, high] inclusive"],["Key Insight","A range count \"between low and high\" splits cleanly into \"at most high\" minus \"at most low minus 1\""],["Constraints","Up to 2 times 10^4 numbers, values up to 2*10^4"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Count pairs whose XOR falls in a range\"","A binary trie built bit by bit (most significant bit first) lets XOR-related counting be done incrementally as numbers are inserted"],["\"Between low and high\" (a range, not a single threshold)","Reduce to two at-most-a-threshold queries and subtract"]]}

blocks.text: Counting pairs with XOR in [low, high] is equivalent to (count of pairs with XOR at most high) minus (count of pairs with XOR at most low minus 1). Each "at most a threshold" count can be computed by inserting numbers one at a time into a binary trie (bit by bit, most significant bit first), and for each new number, walking the trie alongside the threshold's bits to count how many already-inserted numbers would XOR with it to something at most that threshold, all in one pass proportional to the bit width.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting How Many Prior Visitors Fall Within a Height Difference Limit
blocks.text: Picture recording each visitor's height in binary form into a structured cabinet as they arrive, and for each new visitor, quickly tallying how many EARLIER visitors would have a height difference (measured bit by bit as XOR) within an allowed limit, using the structure to avoid comparing against every earlier visitor individually.

blocks.caption: A range count splits into two at-most queries: count(XOR <= high) minus count(XOR <= low minus 1)

blocks.text: Result: 6. Pairs like (1,4) XOR to 5, (1,2) XOR to 3, and others fall within [2,6].

Before checking every pair directly (an O(n squared) scan), notice that XOR is computed bit by bit independently, which is exactly what a binary trie (branching on 0 or 1 at each bit position) is built to exploit: inserting numbers one at a time and querying "how many already-inserted numbers XOR with this one to at most a threshold" can be done in one trie walk per number.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "XOR in range [low, high]" splits into two simpler "XOR at most a threshold" queries, subtracted: countAtMost(high) minus countAtMost(low minus 1).

Observation 2: For a single "at most threshold" query, process numbers one at a time, maintaining a binary trie of ALREADY-INSERTED numbers (most significant bit first).

Observation 3: For each new number, walk the trie alongside the threshold's bits. At each bit position where the threshold has a 1, taking the SAME bit as the current number (making that XOR bit 0, which is already less than the threshold's 1) guarantees every number under that branch satisfies the threshold regardless of remaining bits, so its whole subtree count can be added immediately; then continue down the OPPOSITE bit branch to keep matching the threshold's bits exactly.

Observation 4: Where the threshold has a 0, only the SAME bit as the current number keeps the running XOR at exactly 0 so far (not yet exceeding), so the walk must continue down that single branch, with no immediate count added.

Observation 5: If the walk survives to the very end without running out of trie path, the accumulated XOR along that path equals the threshold EXACTLY, so that final node's count is also added.

This leads to inserting numbers into a binary trie one at a time, walking the trie alongside the threshold's bits before each insertion to accumulate counts, and computing the answer as countAtMost(high) minus countAtMost(low minus 1).
Try every pair of indices directly, computing the XOR and checking if it falls within [low, high].
Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every pair directly implements the definition simply.
This costs O(n squared), far too slow for up to 2*10^4 numbers; a binary trie counts matches for one number against ALL previously inserted numbers in one walk proportional to the bit width.

blocks.text: Limitation: a binary trie, combined with the "at most threshold, subtracted" range trick, brings this down to roughly O(n times bit width).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define countAtMost(nums, limit) using a binary trie: for each number, before inserting it, walk the trie alongside limit's bits (most significant bit first). At a 1-bit of limit, add the count of the SAME-bit child (its subtree all satisfies the bound regardless of further bits), then descend the OPPOSITE-bit child to keep tracking exact equality. At a 0-bit of limit, simply descend the SAME-bit child with no addition. If the walk survives to the end, add that final node's count too (exact equality case). Then insert the number into the trie. The final answer is countAtMost(nums, high) minus countAtMost(nums, low minus 1).
Use a binary trie built incrementally per "at most threshold" query, and compute the range count as a subtraction of two such queries.
Dry run intuition for countAtMost([1,4,2,7], 6) with a few bits

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Number inserted so far","What happens for the next number"],"rows":[["1st number (1)","none yet","No prior numbers, count contribution is 0"],["2nd number (4)","{1}","Trie walk alongside limit=6's bits finds how many prior numbers XOR with 4 to at most 6"],["3rd number (2)","{1,4}","Similarly checks against both prior numbers in one trie walk"],["4th number (7)","{1,4,2}","Checks against all three prior numbers in one trie walk"]]}

blocks.text: The trie walk mirrors the limit's bits exactly: wherever the limit has a 1-bit, choosing the matching bit (XOR contributes 0 there, strictly less than the limit's 1) guarantees the ENTIRE subtree beneath satisfies the bound no matter what the remaining bits are, so its count is safely added in bulk; the walk then follows the opposite branch to keep tracking numbers that could still exactly equal the limit going forward. Wherever the limit has a 0-bit, only matching exactly (XOR contributes 0) keeps the running comparison undecided, so the walk must continue there with no immediate addition. If the walk survives every bit this way, the surviving numbers have XOR exactly equal to the limit, correctly included at the end.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times bit width) for both the counting queries.
Space: O(n times bit width) for the trie.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "count pairs whose XOR falls within a numeric range", think: reduce to two at-most-threshold queries, each solved via a binary trie walked alongside the threshold's bits.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The pairwise-check approach costs O(n squared); the binary-trie approach costs O(n times bit width), the standard efficient solution for XOR-range counting.

items: Pattern: binary trie over bits, combined with a range-to-two-at-most-queries reduction.
Core Idea: XOR is decided bit by bit; a trie walk mirroring the threshold's bits bulk-counts entire subtrees wherever the bound is already guaranteed.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n times bit width) for the trie approach.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n times bit width) for the trie approach.
Most Important Observation: a range count reduces cleanly to two at-most-threshold queries subtracted.
One line memory trick: at-most(high) minus at-most(low minus one), via a bitwise trie walk.
